paragraphs: The author said: When we investigated the most firmly-established of the pillars of our religion and its foundations, we found that the purification of affirming the unity of our Creator (mighty and exalted) is its root and its foundation-stone — for it is the first gate among the gates of the Law, and by affirming-the-unity faith is distinguished from associationism, and it is the very head of the true reality of religion. Whoever has deviated from it — no deed of his is valid, nor is his faith established. That is why the first address of God (mighty and exalted) to us at Mount Sinai was "I am the Lord your God…" (Exodus 20:2) and "You shall have no other gods…" (Exodus 20:3). Then He confirmed it upon us through the hand of His messenger (peace be upon him), in his saying: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4).

You ought, my brother, to grasp the meaning of this passage — I mean *Shemaʿ Yisraʾel* through its end — and see how its speech moves within it from one meaning to another, and that it contains ten meanings corresponding to the Ten Words.

For He commanded us to bind ourselves to verifying-the-reality of the Creator (mighty and exalted) — and that is His saying "Hear, O Israel." By "Hear" He does not intend "listen with the ear," but rather He intended firm conviction and binding-obligation, as Scripture says "We shall do and we shall hear" (Exodus 24:7), and "And you, Israel, shall hear and shall observe to do" (Deuteronomy 5:1). Everything that proceeds in this register, with the term "hearing," intends by it: binding-obligation, firm conviction, and acceptance.

Then, after He had imposed upon us firm conviction in the true reality of His existence, He bound us to be firmly convinced that He is our God and our Lord, by His saying "the Lord is our God." Then He bound us to be firmly convinced that He is truly one, by His saying "the Lord is one."

And once He had imposed upon us firm conviction in these three meanings that we have mentioned, He moved from them to that which we are obligated to follow them with — namely, purity in love of God, with the outward and the inward, with the life-blood and with property — in His saying "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 6:5). I will explicate this concept in the Gate of Love, with the help of God (exalted be He).

Then He moved from this to the reinforcement of the duties of the heart, in His saying "And these words which I command you this day shall be upon your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:6) — which means: bind them within your heart and firmly believe them in your innermost being.

Then He moved from this to the duties of the limbs that comprise both knowledge and action, in His saying "And you shall teach them diligently to your children" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Then He said "and you shall speak of them" — meaning: if you have no child, do not let the absence of a child be a cause for failing to recite them. Then He said "when you sit in your house, and when you walk along the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up" — for the heart and the tongue are never barred from fulfilling their obligations, the way the other limbs may be barred, as I have set out earlier — regarding the perpetual binding force of the duties of the heart — in the opening of this book of mine. All of this is a reinforcement of what came before, of His saying "And these words which I command you this day shall be upon your heart…" — so that the constant repetition of them upon the tongue should compel their constant repetition in the mind, so that the heart may never be empty of remembrance of God — like the saying of David (peace be upon him): "I have set the Lord always before me" (Psalms 16:8), and "For the matter is very near to you…" (Deuteronomy 30:14).

Then He moved from those duties of the limbs that combine knowledge and action to those that are pure action only, dividing them into three categories in His saying: "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes, and you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates" (Deuteronomy 6:8–9) — these being the *tefillin* of the hand, the *tefillin* of the head, and the *mezuzah*. All of these are means for remembrance of the Creator (exalted be He), for the purification of love for Him, and for yearning toward Him — like the words of Scripture concerning the tokens by which lovers remember each other: "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm…" (Song of Songs 8:6), and "Behold, I have engraved you upon the palms of My hands…" (Isaiah 49:16), and "I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, My servant, and I will set you as a signet" (Haggai 2:23), and "A bundle of myrrh is my beloved unto me, that lies between my breasts" (Song of Songs 1:13). He made them three so that they might be the more firm and binding, as the Wise One said: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12).
Thus the totality of what this passage contains is ten meanings: five of them spiritual, and five corporeal.

As for the spiritual: the first is our firm conviction that the Creator exists; the second, that He is our Lord; the third, that He is one; the fourth, the purification of our love for Him; and the fifth, binding ourselves to obedience to Him through purification of the heart.

As for the corporeal: the first is "And you shall teach them diligently to your children"; the second, "and you shall speak of them"; the third, "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand"; the fourth, "and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes"; and the fifth, "and you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates."

And the early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Why does *Shemaʿ* precede *And it shall come to pass if you hearken*? So that one accepts upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven first, and afterwards he accepts upon himself the yoke of the commandments" (m. Berakhot 2:2).
That is why I have judged it right to place the Gate of the Purification of Affirming-the-Unity before all the other gates of this book of mine.
It is now incumbent upon me to explain, concerning the purification of affirming the unity of God, ten concepts:

1. The first: what is the definition of the purification of affirming-the-unity. 2. The second: into how many divisions the concept of affirming-the-unity is divided. 3. The third: whether one is obligated to investigate it by the way of speculative investigation or not. 4. The fourth: the method of investigation into its meaning, and what ought to precede our knowledge of it before the investigation of unity. 5. The fifth: on the establishment of the premises by which it is established that the world has a Creator who created it from nothing. 6. The sixth: on the manner of employing these premises to establish the existence of the Creator. 7. The seventh: on the proof that He is one. 8. The eighth: on the explication of the aspects of the metaphorical One and the True One. 9. The ninth: that the Creator is the True One, and there is no True One other than Him. 10. The tenth: on the divine attributes, both the intelligible and the scriptural, and the aspects according to which their affirmation and negation of Him are valid.
He said: As for the definition of the purification of affirming-the-unity of God (mighty and exalted) —

It is the equivalence of heart and tongue in affirming-the-unity of God (exalted be He), after [one has reached] by inference the soundness of His existence and the true reality of His unity through the way of speculative investigation.
That is because affirming-the-unity of God (mighty and exalted) varies among the rational beings according to the variation in their discernment and their understanding.
Among them is one who affirms-unity of God with his tongue alone — that is, he hears people saying something and follows them in it, with no knowledge of the meaning of what he says.

And among them is one who affirms-unity with his heart and his tongue, and understands the meaning of what he says by way of transmission from his fathers — but has no knowledge of the soundness of what he firmly believes concerning the affirmation of the unity of God.

And among them is one who affirms-unity after he has reached, by inference, [knowledge of] the soundness of this — except that he carries Him in his imagination just as he carries any other single existing things, and so he renders the Creator (exalted) corporeal and represents Him with shape and likeness, on account of his ignorance of the true reality of His unity and the concept of His existence.

And among them is one who affirms-unity with his heart and his tongue, after he has verified-realization in the concept of the True One and the metaphorical One, and has inferred the soundness of His existence and the true reality of His unity — and this is the most complete of the aspects of affirming-unity of God (mighty and exalted).

And that is why I have said, in the definition of the purification of affirming-the-unity, that it is the equivalence of heart and tongue in affirming-the-unity of God, after rational inference for it, and his knowing the aspects of the true reality of His unity through the way of speculative investigation.
He said: As for the divisions into which the affirmation of unity of God (exalted be He) is divided —

I say: Since the term *tawḥīd* has become so widespread in the speech of the people of *tawḥīd*, and they so constantly employ it in their utterances, that it has become for them one of the terms of wonderment uttered both in joy and in affliction — used at moments of grief over misfortune, to magnify and decry it, without reflection on the knowledge of the true reality of what is being declared upon their tongues, out of ignorance and inattention.

They imagine that the meaning of *tawḥīd* is pure within them just as its utterance is pure upon their lips, and they do not perceive that their hearts are empty of its true reality, and their innermost beings are void of its concept. For they affirm-unity with their tongues and their utterances, but firmly believe in their hearts in more than one [god]; and in their innermost beings they represent Him with the form of any single existent thing; and they ascribe to Him attributes that do not befit the True One — on account of their ignorance of the concept of the True One and the metaphorical One. [None grasps it] except for the elite among the people of *tawḥīd* — those who have rooted themselves firmly in knowledge and have understood the meaning of "Creator" and "creature" and the conditions and properties of the True One.

And indeed the philosopher spoke truly when he said: "None worships the Cause of Causes and the First of Firsts except the prophet of the age by his very nature, and the philosopher who has surpassed [his peers] by what he has acquired of knowledge. As for those below these two, they worship only what is less than Him — for they cannot conceive of any existent thing except as composite."
That is why the variation in *tawḥīd* must accord with the variation in people's intellects. And [people] differ in their discernment in *tawḥīd* across four divisions.

**The first** is the affirmation of unity of God by the tongue alone — and this is the first of its degrees, to which the child ascends, and the one ignorant of the meaning of religion, with no reality to its meaning in his soul.

**The second division** is the affirmation of unity of God by heart and tongue, on the basis of imitation and good faith in tradition — with no knowledge of the soundness of this from the side of his intellect and understanding. He is in the position of a blind man led by one of sound sight — and perhaps he imitates someone else who is himself an imitator. So they are in the position of a group of blind men, each of whom has placed his hand upon the shoulder of his companion, and his companion the same upon the shoulder of the one next to him, until the matter ends at the first of them — the one of sound sight, who leads them. If the leader is heedless in his care for them, or fails in his looking out for them, or one of them stumbles, or some calamity befalls him, the defect overtakes them all, and they go astray from their path; and perhaps they fall into a pit, or stumble against something that hinders them from proceeding.

So too is the imitator in his affirmation of unity: he is not safe from associationism. And if he hears something from the speech of the unbelievers and their arguments, perhaps his school will be inverted, and he will fall into unbelief without noticing it. That is why our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Be diligent to learn how to answer the heretic" (m. Avot 2:14).

**The third division** of the divisions of *tawḥīd* is the affirmation of unity of God by heart and tongue, after inference for it and for the soundness of His existence by the way of speculative investigation — but without knowledge of the meaning of the True One and the metaphorical One. He is in the position of a man of sound sight, walking on a road, intending a distant city. The road has many points of confusion, and he does not know it, nor can he distinguish the shortest of the roads to the city he is making for — though he knows the direction and the region [in which it lies]. He wears himself out greatly and does not reach what he seeks, on account of his ignorance of the road — as the Wise One said: "The toil of fools wearies them, for he does not know how to go to the city" (Ecclesiastes 10:15).

**The fourth division** is the affirmation of unity of God (mighty and exalted) by heart and tongue, after inference for it and his standing upon the true reality of His unity by way of speculative investigation and the use of intellectual demonstration. And this is the most complete of them, and the highest. The Messenger (peace be upon him) urged upon it in his saying: "And you shall know this day, and lay it upon your heart, that the Lord, He is God" (Deuteronomy 4:39).
He said: As for the question — whether we are obligated to investigate the affirmation of unity by the way of speculative investigation, or not —

I say: Anyone for whom it is possible to investigate this concept, and others like it among the intelligibles, by the way of intellectual demonstration, is obligated to investigate it according to his apprehension and the force of his discernment. What I have set down at the opening of this book of mine concerning the necessity and the obligation of this is sufficient.

As for one who is heedless of investigating its soundness and its certainty: he is held to account for his heedlessness regarding it, and joined to the rank of those who fall short in their knowledge and in their action. In this he is like an intelligent sick man who knows about disease and remedy, who entrusts himself to a physician treating him with various kinds of treatment — yet is too lazy to make use of his own understanding and judgment in following the physician's treatment of him, so as to know whether the treatment of his illness is correct or in error, without any obstacle preventing him from this.

And the Book has bound us to this, in its saying: "And you shall know this day, and bring it back to your heart, that the Lord, He is God in the heavens above and on the earth below; there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39). The proof that *bringing back to the heart* intends *the use of the intellect* is the saying of the Book: "And no one brings it to his heart, nor [has] knowledge, nor understanding…" (Isaiah 44:19). And the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart…" (1 Chronicles 28:9). And he said: "Know that the Lord, He is God…" (Psalms 100:3). And the Prophet said: "Have you not known? Have you not heard? The eternal God, the Lord…" (Isaiah 40:28). And He said: "I will set him on high, because he has known my name" (Psalms 91:14). And He said: "But let him that boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows me" (Jeremiah 9:23). And our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "Be diligent to learn how to answer the heretic" (m. Avot 2:14). And the Book said: "You shall observe and you shall do, for this is your wisdom and your understanding [in the sight of the peoples]" (Deuteronomy 4:6).

For the acknowledgment of the nations to us — [of our possessing] wisdom and understanding — will not be sound except through their bearing witness to the demonstrative proofs and the rational evidence for the soundness of our Book and the certainty of our doctrine. And God has promised us the lifting of the veils of ignorance from the intellects of the nations, and the manifestation of His dazzling light as proof to us of the soundness of our religion, as He said: "And many nations shall go and say: 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, that He may teach us of His ways, and we shall walk in His paths'" (Isaiah 2:3).

Thus the soundness of the obligation of speculative investigation, in whatever we are capable of apprehending the soundness of by our intellects, has been established for us from the rational, the scriptural, and the transmitted.
He said: As for the method of investigating into the true reality of affirming-the-unity, and what ought to precede our knowledge of it before the investigation of affirming-the-unity —

I say: With every object whose knowledge is sought: if its existence is doubtful, then one asks of it, *is it, or is it not*. And if its existence has been established, one investigates concerning it *what* it is, and *how* it is, and *why* it is. But as for the Creator (exalted be He), the question concerning Him is permitted only as *is He*, alone.

So once His existence has been established by the way of speculative investigation, we investigate concerning Him: *is He one, or more than one*. And once we have verified-the-reality that He is one, we investigate the meaning of *one* — in how many senses *one* is predicated of that of which it is predicated. By this the complete and purified affirmation of unity will be established for us, in accord with what the Book has said: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4).

For this reason it is incumbent upon us to investigate, first, whether this world has a Creator or not. And once it is established for us that this world has a Creator who created it and brought it into being, we investigate concerning Him: is He one, or more than one. And once it is established for us that He is one, we investigate the meaning of the metaphorical One and the True One, and what of His true meaning may be predicated of the Creator. And at that point the concept of affirming-the-unity is brought to completion in our hearts and purified in our innermost beings — by the help of God and His support.
He said: As for the premises by which it is established that the world has a Creator who created it from nothing — they are three premises.
The first: that a thing does not make itself.
The second premise: that the principles [of existents] are finite in number, and have a first beginning before which there is no [other] beginning.
The third premise: that every composite is originated [in time].

When the soundness of these three premises has been established, it follows from them — for one who knows how to handle and combine them properly — that the world has a Creator who created it from nothing, as we shall expound in what follows, with the help of God.
As for the proof of the soundness of these three premises, it runs as I shall describe — and that is as follows:

[*Proof of the first premise.*] Every existent that comes to be after non-being can come about in only one of two ways: either it brought itself into existence, or something other than it brought it into existence. And anything we might imagine to have made itself can be conceived only as making itself either *after* its own being, or *before* its own being — and both are impossible. For if it made itself after its own being, then its prior being has already rendered the act of self-making superfluous, and so it made nothing. And if it made itself before its own being, then in that moment it was non-existent, and a non-existent admits of no action and no abstention — for the non-existent makes nothing. Thus it is impossible, in any of its aspects, that a thing make itself. So the first premise that we set down is established.

[*Proof of the second premise.*] Everything that has an end has a beginning — for it has been established that whatever has no beginning has no end. For from a thing without a first, no [counted advance] reaches a limit at which a person can come to rest; so whenever we have found a *last* for something, we have known that it had a *first* before which there was no first, and a *beginning* before which there was no beginning. Now since we have stopped at the end of [a chain of] principles of the existing things in this world, we know that they had a first before which there was no first, and a beginning before which there was no beginning — for principles cannot be without limit at the start.

Further: it is known that everything that has a part has a whole, since the whole is nothing but the totality of its parts; and it is impossible that there should be any *part* of what is without limit. For the definition of *part* is "a magnitude separated from a [greater] magnitude, the smaller measuring the larger," in the manner of Euclid's definition at the opening of Book V of his treatise on geometry. And if we suppose something to be infinite in actuality and we separate from it some portion, the remainder must inevitably be less than what it was before. If the remainder is itself infinite, then what was without limit was greater than what is without limit — and this is impossible. And if the remainder is finite, then when we add to it the separated portion (which is finite), the whole is finite — but we had described it at first as infinite, so it is at once finite and infinite, and this is an absurdity that cannot stand. Therefore it is not permissible that a *part* be separated from the infinite — so whatever has a part is, inevitably, finite. Now if we mentally subtract from those who came forth into being in this world — from the time of Noah to the time of Moses (peace be upon them) — that segment, it is a part of the totality of the individuals of the world, and it is finite. Hence the totality is finite in number. And since the totality of this world is finite, it follows that its [originating] principles too are finite in number — and so this world must have a first before which there is no first, by necessity. And from this the finitude of the principles at the beginning has been established, as we set out.

[*Proof of the third premise.*] Every composite is necessarily put together out of things more than one, and those things from which it is composed are prior to it by *natural* priority, and therefore its composer must be prior to it by both natural and temporal priority. Now *the eternal* is that which has no cause, and what has no cause has no beginning, and what has no beginning has no end. Whatever has a beginning is not eternal, and whatever is not eternal is originated — for between *the eternal* and *the originated* there is no middle term that would be neither eternal nor originated. Therefore every composite, since it is not eternal, must necessarily be originated. Thus the third premise that we mentioned has been established.
He said: As for the ways of handling the premises that we have set forth, in order to verify-the-reality of the existence of the Creator (mighty and exalted) —

That is as follows: when we look attentively at this world, we find it composed and compounded, and no part of its parts is free from composition and ordering. For we see — with our senses and our intellects — that it is like a house built and prepared with all its furnishings: the sky above it like a roof, the earth spread out like a carpet, the stars arranged like its lamps, the precious stones laid up in store like its treasures, each thing in its proper place; man like the householder using what is in it; the various kinds of plants made ready for his interests, and the species of animal disposed for his benefit — as the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "You made him to rule over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, all of them, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, the fish of the sea, that pass through the paths of the seas" (Psalms 8:7–9).

Then [we observe] the ordering of the sun's rising and setting, to establish the alternation of the rule of day and night; and the rising and falling of the sun, to establish the times of spring and summer and autumn and winter — the conditions of the times of the year and their benefits, and the sun's passing along a single unbroken continuous order, as He said: "Who commands the sun and it does not rise, and seals up the stars" (Job 9:7), and "You make darkness and it is night" (Psalms 104:20). Then the rotation of the spheres — of varying motions — and the wandering stars and the constellations moving by a measured arrangement and a precise weight that does not break down nor go astray; with every one of them intended toward a use and a benefit for the rational beings, as the Wise One said: "He has made everything beautiful in its time" (Ecclesiastes 3:11), and "To everything there is a season, and a time to every purpose under heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). All of this exhibits manifest composition and compounding in the whole and in its parts.

Then, when we examine the plants and the animals, we find them composed of the four elements — I mean fire and air and water and earth. These elements are different from each other and mutually opposed; we have no means of composing and ordering them by the natural-order [we observe], since they are transmuted into one another, and one repels the other. Whenever we bind some of them together, they hurry off into transmutation and transition. Yet nature's composing of them is firm and stable, for a determined span.

Some of the philosophers have claimed that the celestial spheres and the stars and the higher individual bodies are of the nature of fire — like the saying of the friend [of God] (peace be upon him): "Who makes His messengers winds, His ministers a flaming fire" (Psalms 104:4); and in this saying there is evidence for the soundness of this view. And it is not a *fifth nature*, as Aristotle claimed.

Thus, since the existing things are constituted out of the elements and composed of them, and we know that they have not blended themselves by themselves, nor have they composed themselves by their own natures (because of the opposition of one to another) — it has come first to our intellects and been established in our souls that their composer is other than they, their binder is other than they, and that the one who composes them on a basis contrary to their natures — indeed, by constraint upon them — is their Creator (mighty and exalted), who has firmly bound them together and skillfully composed them.

And when we investigate the four elements, we find them also composed — out of matter and form, which are substance and accident. As for their *matter*: it is the prime matter that bears the four elements, *hayūlā*. As for their *form*: it is the first universal form, which is the root of every substantial form and every accidental form — such as heat, cold, moisture, dryness, heaviness, lightness, motion, rest, and the like.

Composition and compounding, then, are manifest in the totality of the world and in all its parts, in its roots and its branches, in its simples and its compounds, in its higher portions and its lower. So it follows from what we have set down before that the whole of it must be originated, in accord with what has been established for us — that every composite is originated. Hence we are bound to firmly believe that the world is originated.

And since this is so, and it is impossible that a thing should make itself, it follows that the world must have a Maker who brought it into being and originated it. And since it is established that the [chain of] principles cannot be without a limit at the start, it follows that the world must have a beginning before which there is no beginning, and a first before which there is no first; and He is the one who created it and originated it: *not from anything, not by anything, not upon anything* — in line with the saying of the Book on this meaning: "I am the Lord, who makes all things, who stretches out the heavens alone, who spreads out the earth by Myself" (Isaiah 44:24), and "He stretches out the north over the void; He hangs the earth upon nothing" (Job 26:7). And He is the Maker (mighty and exalted), whom we have sought and toward whose existence we have aimed by our thoughts and our intellects; He is the Eternal — to whose priority there is no beginning, and the Everlasting whose precedence has no end — as He said: "I am the First, and I am the Last" (Isaiah 44:6), and: "I am the Lord, the First; and with the last, I am He" (Isaiah 41:4).

Now a certain people have claimed that the world came together at the beginning of its being by chance and accident, without any Creator inaugurating it or any Originator originating it. And it is, in my view, a wonder that a view of this kind could find passage in a rational being's mind in a state of soundness. For if the holder of this position were to hear someone else say something like it concerning a waterwheel that turns to irrigate a plot of land — were that other person to claim that the waterwheel had come together without any artisan having undertaken its composition and construction, and the proper placement of each of its parts toward the end of its usefulness — he would denounce the claim as outrageous, and ascribe to its holder the utmost limit of ignorance, and hurry to declare him a liar and his statement absurd. Yet if such a claim is impossible, in his judgment, regarding *a paltry, contemptible waterwheel made by a brief contrivance for the use of a small plot of land*: how does he allow himself to firmly believe its like concerning *this greater wheel that encompasses the earth and all the creatures upon it* — fashioned with a wisdom and a power before whose true essence the intellects of human beings and the understandings of rational creatures fall short, and prepared for the benefit of all the earth and what is in it and what is upon it? How is it permissible for him to say of it that it came together without the aim of an aiming-purpose, and the governance of a wise and powerful one?

It is known to us that things which are devoid of the aim of an aiming-purpose in any part of them cannot give any room to the trace of wisdom or power. Do you not see: if a man were to spill ink upon a sheet of paper in a single jet, no ordered book or readable lines could be configured upon it as those that come about by means of the pen. And if someone were to bring us a composed book that could not have been arranged without the agency of a pen, and were to claim that he had spilled ink upon the paper and the writing was configured upon it of its own accord — we would hurry to declare him a liar, and [to claim] that it cannot have come about apart from the aim of an aiming-purpose. So if it is impossible to us that ordered letters be sketched out without our deliberate convention — how, in the case of what is finer in workmanship and more remote in measure to a degree without limit in our reckoning, would it be allowable to say that it has come together without the aim of an aiming-purpose, and the wisdom of a wise one, and the power of a powerful one?

In what we have offered for the establishment of the existence of the Creator (exalted be He) by way of His traces, there is sufficiency for one who understands and judges fairly — and in this there is sufficient response and refutation against the *dahriyya*, who firmly believe that the world is eternal. Understand this!
He said: As for the proof that the Creator (exalted be He) is one —

That is as follows: since it has been established for us, by the way of inference, that the world has a Creator, it is incumbent upon us to investigate concerning Him: *is He one, or more than one*. So we ought to set out the soundness of His oneness from seven aspects.

**The first** — through our reflection on the causes of existents. For when we sift through them, we find them less in number than their effects; and whenever we investigate the causes of those causes, ascending, we find them, again, less in number than them; and the higher we ascend, the smaller their number, until they end at a single cause — and that is the Cause of Causes.

The explanation of this: the *individuals* of the existing things are not finite in number, but when we abstract their containing *species*, those are fewer in number than [the individuals] under them — for every species contains many individuals — and the species are finite in number. Then if we ascend [from] the species to their containing *genera*, the genera are fewer than the species — for under every one of the genera there are many species; and so on the further we ascend, the genera are fewer in number, until they end at the *genera of the genera*. And the Philosopher has said that the genera of the genera are ten — and they are: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, possession, action, and being-acted-upon.

When we then investigate the causes of the individuals of the species of these ten genera, we find them five: motion, and the four elements (fire, air, water, earth). When we investigate the causes of the four elements, we find them matter and form — two. When we investigate the cause of these two, it must inevitably be fewer than two — and that is the will of the Creator (exalted be He); and there is no number less than two except *one*. So the Creator (exalted be He), of necessity from this aspect, is One. And the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "Yours, O Lord, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head above all" (1 Chronicles 29:11) — meaning by this: the most lifted up of all that is lifted up, the most high of all that is high, the first of every beginning, the cause of every cause and every caused thing.

**The second aspect** — through the trace of the manifest wisdom in this whole world, in its highest and its lowest, in its mineral and its plant and its animal. When we look attentively at it, it indicates to us that the whole of it is *the governance of a single Governor* and *the artifact of a single Maker*. For we find it, despite its variation in its roots and its elements, similar in its branches and resembling itself in its parts; the traces of the wisdom of the Creator (mighty and exalted) manifest in the small and the great of the creation, bearing witness that it [comes] from a single wise Creator.

If the world were of more than one creator, the form of the wisdom in the parts of the world would vary, and contradict itself in its wholes and its particulars. Moreover, we find the world's parts in need of one another for their permanence and their subsistence and their well-being; no part of it is complete except by another part — as the rings of mail-armor stand in need of each other, and the parts of the bed, and the limbs of a human body, and all other composites stand in need of each other for their constitution and their completion. Do you not see the need of the moon and the stars for the light of the sun? And the need of the earth for the heaven and the water? And the need of the animal kinds for each other (since some species feed on others, like the birds of prey and predatory fish and the wild beasts of the land)? And the need of man for the whole, and the constitution of the whole through man? And the need of the lands and the climes and the sciences and the crafts for each other?

Wisdom is manifest in the fine and the great of creation, in its small and in its large. For the trace of the wisdom and power manifest in the creation of the elephant, despite the magnitude of its body, is no more wondrous than the trace of the wisdom manifest in the creation of the ant and the gnat, for all their smallness — indeed, the smaller the creation, the more manifest is the trace of wisdom and power in it, and the subtle artistry of the Maker is more wondrous and more evident in it. All this indicates that the whole of it is the governance of a single Governor and a single Creator — by virtue of its similarity and its harmonious agreement and its convergence upon the completion of the world's order and the constitution of its totality through all its parts. If it were of more than one creator, the form of the wisdom would vary in some parts of the world, and some [parts] would dispense with others. But since it is varied in its roots and its elements, [yet] in agreement in its branches and its composites, that indicates that its originator, and its composer, and its director, and its governor, is one.

And the Philosopher said: *Nothing that God created is stranger than what God created* — meaning that the wisdom in the fine and the great, the small and the large, of the world's parts, is similar and well-matched. As the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said, in describing the kinds of traces of wisdom and the order of [the world's] construction: "How manifold are Your works, O Lord! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your possessions" (Psalms 104:24); and: "How great are Your works, O Lord! Your thoughts are very deep" (Psalms 92:6).

**The third aspect** — from the general origination of the totality of the world. The proofs have already shown that the world is originated, and it follows from this that it must have an originator, since it is impossible for a thing to bring itself into being. So when we find an originated thing, and it has been established for us that *it was after it was not*, we know, by the testimony of sound intellects, that something other than itself originated and produced it. And once it has been established that the world has a Creator who originated it, it is not permissible for us to firmly believe in more than one — since *one* Creator is indispensable, but *more than one* is not needed. Were it possible for the existence and stability of the world to be established in our intellects on the basis of *fewer than one* creator, we would believe that; but since we cannot conceive of anything that admits of its being produced by another smaller in number than one, we know with necessary knowledge that He is one.

[The general principle:] Things whose soundness is to be established by the way of inference, and whose existence is *necessary* [for the explanation of an observed effect], we are not obligated to firmly believe in any *more* than what necessity demands toward the completion of the thing being inferred. The example is this: if we see a book that is uniform in its order, and the shape of the script in which it is written is one shape, it occurs to our intellects that *a single writer* wrote it and arranged it. For the book is not soundly nor completely accounted for by *fewer than one writer* — and were its having been written by fewer than one writer possible, we would believe even that. And though it is *possible* that more than one wrote it, it is not permissible for us to firmly believe that of it without evidence to bear witness to its soundness — such as variations in the form of the writing in some part of it, or the like.

Since this is so, and the writer of the book is not directly observed by us at the moment of writing — neither before nor after — we are dispensed from witnessing him in his own person, in particular, by our witnessing of *the writing*; and the inference from his act and from the arrangement of his book takes the place of direct observation of him. We know by necessity that *a writer*, existing, knowing how to write and able to do it, wrote that book — and that no one else shared with him in it, on account of its order and balance. For the work of multiple agents is varied, not arranged and balanced, but mutually-opposed, not well-made and firmly-bound.

The same applies to the discourse on the Creator of the world (exalted be He). Since the traces of His wisdom in His creatures are resembling and similar, necessity calls for the belief in one Creator who created it — for one Creator is necessary in the existence of originated things, and He is not, exalted be He, a thing that is *seen* — like substance and accident. And since He (mighty and exalted) is not seen, the soundness of His existence and the soundness of belief in Him can only be established by inference and by drawing-inference from His creatures. So our belief in His existence — and that He is *one*, *eternal*, *who has never ceased and will never cease*; *mighty*, *wise*, *living* — stands in the place of direct observation of Him (exalted is He above that, for He is not of the order of visible things).

Hence necessity calls for the belief in one Creator who created the world, since [one such] is indispensable in the existence of the originated things, while *more than one* is dispensable and unneeded. Whoever claims that He is *more than one*, his statement cannot be sound except on the basis of *some evidence other than the evidence we have set forth*. And there is no way to establish that, due to the impossibility of the rational evidences contradicting each other. Rather, all the evidences bear witness to His unity, and exclude from Him the meanings of *plurality, partnership, and likeness* — corresponding to His saying (exalted is He): "Is there any God beside Me? Yea, there is no Rock; I know not any" (Isaiah 44:8), and: "I, even I, am He; I am the First, and I am also the Last; My hand also has laid the foundation of the earth, and My right hand has spanned the heavens; when I call to them, they stand up together" (Isaiah 48:12–13), and: "A righteous God and a Savior, there is none beside Me" (Isaiah 45:21).

**The fourth aspect.** I would say to one who firmly believed that the Creator is more than one: either the essence of the totality [of them] is a single essence, or it is not one. If he says the essence is one, then the meaning is, in that case, one — and the Creator is not *more than one*. And if he says that each one of them has an essence other than the essence of the other, then it follows of necessity that between them there is a *distinction* — for their otherness and their variance. And every distinct thing is bounded; and every bounded thing is finite; and every finite thing is composite; and every composite is originated; and every originated thing has an originator. So whoever claims that the Creator of the world is more than one, it follows that He is originated. But it has been established earlier in our discussion that the Creator of the world is eternal, and is the Cause of Causes and the First of Firsts. Hence He, of necessity, is one — corresponding to the friend [of God] (peace be upon him): "You are He, the Lord, You alone" (Nehemiah 9:6).

**The fifth aspect** — from the meaning of multiplicity and unity. Euclid has defined unity in his book, saying: *Unity is that by which everything is said to be 'one'*. He means that *unity* is naturally prior to *the one* — just as we say that *heat* is prior to *the hot thing*. Were it not for unity, no thing would be said to be one. The meaning that our intellects form of *unity* is *pure singling-out and an exclusiveness into which no resemblance, no sharing in any state whatever, no multiplicity, no number in any aspect, no contiguity to a thing, and no separation from a thing enters*. The meaning of *multiplicity* is *a totality of single ones* — and it is not possible that multiplicity precede the unity from which the multiplicity multiplied. Whatever multiplicity we find with our senses or with our intellects, we know with certain knowledge that unity is prior to it — just as the numerical *one* is prior to the rest of the numbers.

So if anyone claims that the Creator is more than one, he is committed to believing that *the one* is prior, and more antecedent, to all of them — by the priority of *one* to *number*, and of *unity* to *multiplicity*. The Creator, then, is one in every aspect, eternal — there is no eternal-one apart from Him — as He has said (exalted is He): "Before Me no god was formed, neither shall there be after Me" (Isaiah 43:10).

**The sixth aspect** — from the accident that necessarily attaches to every multiple thing. For multiplicity, that is, totality, is an accident attaching to substance — namely, *quantity*. The Creator of substance and accident: no attribute of theirs attaches to His essence. Since the elevation of the Creator above all likening and image-making by means of any of His creatures has been established, both from the rational and from the scriptural [sources], and since the multiplication that attaches to substance is an accident — it is not permitted that any attribute of multiplicity attach to the Creator (exalted be He). And if He is not described by multiplicity, He is *the One*, by necessity — for between unity and multiplicity there is no middle term. Since the Creator is not more than one, He, of necessity, is one — corresponding to Hannah's saying: "There is no holy one like the Lord, for there is none beside You" (1 Samuel 2:2).

**The seventh aspect.** If the Creator were more than one, then either each one of them was [in himself] capable of creating the world, or [each] was not capable of that except by the aid of another. If each was capable of it, then the Creator of the world is *one* — since He is capable of it, having no need of another's aid. And if it could not be accomplished except by their joint operation, then no one of them is complete in strength and power, for each one of them is impotent and falls short; and each one of them is therefore weak. Now every weak thing is finite in strength and in essence; and every finite thing is bounded; and every bounded thing is composite; and every composite is originated; and every originated thing has an originator. So the weak cannot be eternal — for the eternal cannot be incapable of anything, nor in need of the aid of another. Therefore the Creator is not more than one.

And if it were permissible that He be more than one, it would be possible for there to be among them mutual obstruction and disagreement in the creation of the creatures — so that the creation of the world could not be brought to completion from them. But in our finding *this very world* on one order and one motion attaching to every part of its parts (not differing across the ages), we know that its Creator and its Governor and its Director is one — none disputing His action nor undoing His governance. As He (exalted is He) has said: "Who, like Me, can proclaim — let him declare it, and lay it out for Me…" (Isaiah 44:7); and as the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "Forever, O Lord, Your word is established in the heavens; Your faithfulness endures unto all generations; You have founded the earth, and it abides" (Psalms 119:89–90).

What we observe in the traces of God's governance of the creatures [shows] that governance is not perfected, and does not endure on one stable state, except by the *isolation of a single person* in counsel and governance and oversight — like the king in the city, and the soul in the body. And Aristotle said, in his book on this very subject — I mean affirming-the-unity: "*There is no good in the multiplicity of rulers; the ruler must be one.*" And the Wise One said: "When a land transgresses, it has many rulers; but by a man of understanding [and] knowledge its [stability] is prolonged" (Proverbs 28:2).

In what we have set forth on this matter there is sufficiency for one who understands. And in it there is sufficient refutation of the doctrine of the *dualists* and of the Christians in the Trinity, and of others. For in our establishing the unity of the Creator of the world (mighty and exalted), the claim of everyone who has claimed Him to be more than one is annulled. Understand this!
He said: As for the explication of the aspects of the True One and the metaphorical One —

That is as follows: *the one* is a noun derived from *unity*, and it is said in two senses: one of them *accidental* — and that is the metaphorical; the second *substantial* and *stable* — and that is the True.
The accidental *one* is itself of two kinds.

The first kind is that whose multiplicity and totality and aggregation is manifest — such as a single genus that comprehends many species, a single species that comprehends many individuals, a single individual that is composed of many parts, a single army that is an aggregate of people; and such as our saying "one *mudd*," "one *qafīz*," "one *rubʿ*," "one *raṭl*" — each of which covers a totality of things, each of which is called *one*. So each one of the things we have mentioned is called *one* by way of metaphor — by way of the convergence of those things that are gathered by that name into a single meaning. And it is called *many* by way of what it contains — namely, many things. When those things are divided and separated, each of them is called *one*. So *the one* in such matters as we have mentioned is an accident — it is *one* from one angle and *many* from another angle.

The second kind of the accidental *one* is *the one* predicated of a single individual: he is not multiplied, nor is he general for an aggregate of things in his outward appearance — but he is *many in his essence*, from the angle of his being composed of matter and form, substance and accident. He admits of generation and corruption, partition, transmutation, conjunction and separation, change, variance, and sharing. So multiplication attaches to a thing said to be *one* from any of the [aspects] we have described — since all these are the contraries of unity. Hence the *one* predicated of a thing in which any of the modes of multiplication or transmutation attach to its essence is, inevitably, an accident — and it is *one* by way of metaphor, not by way of true reality. Understand this!
As for the True One, it too is said in two senses: one of them by *imagination*, and the second by *actuality*.

As for the imaginal — that is the numerical *one*, which is the root and the beginning of number. The meaning of the numerical *one* is *a name and a sign for a beginning before which there is no [other] beginning*; since every true beginning is called *one* — as the Book says: "And there was evening, and there was morning, *day one*" (Genesis 1:5). In the place of "*the first day*," it said "*day one*" — from the angle that *one* is the name for every beginning before which there is no beginning. When [the one] is doubled, it is called "two"; when tripled, "three"; and so on to ten. Then it returns again to *one* [in the next cycle], then to a hundred, and to a thousand, to what has no end of number. For this reason the definition of *number* is *a totality composed of units*. I have called this *imaginal* because *number* does not fall under the bodily senses; rather, it is apprehended by the *wahm* alone — whereas the *numbered* is perceived by the five bodily senses, or by some of them.

The second kind, which is the True One existing in actuality — He is the meaning that does not multiply, does not change, does not transmute; is not described by any attribute of the attributes of bodies; admits no generation, no corruption, no finitude; does not transition and does not move; resembles nothing and nothing resembles Him; shares with nothing. For He is, in whatever way you apprehend Him, *pure one*, and He is the root of every multiplied thing — in accord with what we said earlier: that *unity* is the cause of multiplicity. There is no beginning to the True One, nor end — for everything that has a beginning and end is liable to the entry of generation and corruption upon it; and everything that admits generation and corruption is changeable; and *otherness* is the opposite of unity. So [if there were beginning or end in Him], there would be *more than one* — for what He is before the beginning would be other than what He is after [the beginning]; and so multiplicity would be obligatory for Him. Likewise, *resemblance* in a resembled is an accident, and every thing that bears accidents is multiplied. So the True One has nothing of accidence attaching to His essence in any way.

Now if a speaker should say: "the *unity* in the True One is [itself] an accident," — we would reply: the meaning of unity in the True One is *the denial of multiplication and multiplicity from Him*. So when we describe the One by an attribute, we describe Him only by *the meaning of the absence of multiplication and multiplicity*. The True One is not described by any attribute that would entail multiplication or change or partition or transmutation in His essence, in any way.
This is the entirety of the discourse on the metaphorical one and the True One. Understand this!
He said: As for the proof that the Creator (exalted be He) is the True One, and there is no True One other than Him —

We say: Since every composite cannot come into being except by the *sharing* of its parts from which it is composed (which is the union of some of them with others, and the root of sharing is *unity*) — and likewise the existence of the composite cannot be brought to completion except by the *variance* of its parts out of which it is composed, since composition is only of things more-than-one (and the root of variance is *multiplicity*) — and since the trace of composition and compounding and ordering is found in this world, in its wholes and its particulars and its roots and its branches, it follows that in all of these the meaning of *sharing* and *variance* is found; and the roots of these two are *unity* and *multiplicity*. Since unity is prior by nature to multiplicity — just as the *one* is prior to the rest of numbers — it follows that the cause of multiplied things, at the beginning of principles, must not be multiplied — on account of the priority of the meaning of unity to every multiplied thing.

And since the causes are finite at the beginning, and it is impossible that the Maker make the like of Himself, it is not permitted that the cause of multiplicity-and-unity be like them — I mean *multiplicity-and-unity*. So if the cause of generated things is neither *multiplicity* alone nor *multiplicity-and-unity*, it must be that the cause of being is *one*, True. And we have set down earlier in our discussion that the causes, the further they ascend toward the beginning, the smaller their number, until they end at the root of number — and that is the True One; and that is the Creator (exalted be He).

It is also known that everything found in something *accidentally* must also be found in something else *substantially and truly* — there is no transition for it out of [that thing] except by [that thing's] perishing. Thus heat in hot water is an accident in the water, but in fire it is essential and stable. So too moisture, in [other] bodies, is an accident in them, but in water it is essential and stable. It is also known that everything found accidentally in something acquires that accidence from the thing in which it is essential — as we observe in the heat of hot water (which is an accident in it): the heat was acquired from the fire in which heat is essential. And we observe the moisture of moist bodies, which is in them accidentally, that it is acquired from water, in which moisture is essential. And the rest of the generated things, when we consider them, [run] on this analogy.

On this analogical reasoning the discourse on the meaning of unity proceeds. Since unity in every one of the creatures is accidental (as we have set down), it must be that unity in the cause of the creatures is *essential, stable, true*; and from it the generated things have acquired the accidental meaning of unity, as we explained.

Now when we investigated the meaning of pure unity in the creatures, we did not find it in any one of them as stable and true. Even though every one of the genera, the species, the individuals, the substances, the accidents, the higher bodies, the spiritual substances, and every number and numbered, every finite and bounded thing — is called *one*, and the meaning of unity is ascribed to it — it is called *one* only metaphorically: in that it is *a totality of things* called *one* on the basis of their convergence and resemblance in some meaning; yet it is *many* in its essence, because it admits multiplication, partition, change, variance, composition, dissolution, increase, decrease, motion, transmutation, likening, shaping — and all the other accidents, the special and the general, that attach to every one of the creatures. So pure unity is not found, and is not predicated by way of true reality, of any of the creatures.

And since unity is found in the creatures accidentally, and the evidence and demonstration have shown that the Creator is one — we know, with certain knowledge, that the unity which we have applied to each of the classes of the creatures metaphorically is *acquired from the meaning of the True One*. And pure unity is what is properly ascribed to the Creator of the All (exalted and sanctified). He is the True One — and there is no True One other than Him, as we have established — and all the conditions of *the One* that we have mentioned do not befit, do not properly belong to, anything but Him.

Likewise, all the kinds of multiplication, accidence, transmutation, motion, likening — and everything that does not befit the True One — are denied of Him, in line with the saying of the friend [of God] (peace be upon him): "Many are the wonderful works You have done, O Lord my God, and Your thoughts toward us; there is none to compare with You" (Psalms 40:6); and: "'To whom, then, will you liken Me, that I should be equal?' says the Holy One" (Isaiah 40:25); and: "To whom, then, will you liken God? Or what likeness will you compare unto Him?" (Isaiah 40:18); and: "There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours" (Psalms 86:8); and: "Forasmuch as there is none like You, O Lord, You are great, and Your name is great in might" (Jeremiah 10:6).

So it has been established and made clear that the Creator of the world (exalted be He) is True One, and that there is no True One other than Him: for everything else upon which the name *one* falls — apart from the Creator — though it be *one* from some aspect, is *many* from another aspect, as we have mentioned. But the Creator (exalted be He) is one *in every aspect*, as we have set out. In what we have offered on this matter there is sufficiency for one who understands.

He said: As for the explication of the divine attributes, both the intelligible and the scriptural, by which the Creator (exalted be He) is described, and the purpose intended by them — they are very many, in accord with the creatures and the general benefits given to them. And they are divided into two divisions: *essential* and *active*.

The meaning of our saying "essential": they are attributes stable to God (exalted be He) before the creatures and after them, [attributes] which He deserves by His own essence and selfsame being. They are three attributes — namely, that He (exalted) is *existent*, that He is *one*, and that He is *eternal, with no beginning*.

The purpose in our describing Him with these attributes is to express His meaning and to verify His existence, to give the alert of Him and to make rational beings understand that they have a Creator whom they are obligated to worship and obey.

As for the necessity of describing Him as *existent* — the proofs have shown His existence by direct observation of His traces in the world, in line with the saying of the Book: "Lift your eyes on high, and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of His might, and because He is strong in power, not one is missing" (Isaiah 40:26). So we are required to describe Him as *existent*, since it has been established in our intellects that the non-existent cannot act and from him no command can proceed; and since His traces and creatures have been established as real, the soundness of His existence is established in our intellects.

As for our describing Him with *eternity-without-beginning* and *everlastingness* — the proofs have shown that this world has a first before which there is no first, a beginning before which there is no beginning; and it has been established that the [chain of] principles cannot be other than finite in number at the start; hence it follows of necessity that the Creator of the world has a first before which there is no first — and that is the meaning of *eternity-without-beginning*, in line with the saying of the Book: "From everlasting and to everlasting You are God" (Psalms 90:2), and: "Before Me no god was formed, neither shall there be after Me" (Isaiah 43:10).

As for our describing Him as *one* — we have set this out in the clear proofs [of Chapters 7–9 above], and it has been established by the manifest evidences that the meaning of pure unity is necessarily-attached to His essence; the meaning of *one* is *the denial from His essence of multiplication*, and the impossibility of change, transmutation, accidents, generation and corruption, conjunction and separation, resemblance, sharing, and variance from the true reality of His essence — and the rest of the boundaries of multiplicity.

You ought, my brother, to understand of these attributes that they do not entail change or division in the essence of the Creator (exalted be He). Their meaning is the *denial of their contraries* from the Creator (exalted be He). What is achieved from their meaning, in our intellects and our understandings, is that the Creator (exalted be He) is *not multiple*, *not non-existent*, *not originated*.

Likewise, you ought to know that each one of these three attributes that we have mentioned entails the rest of them when its meaning has been grasped. The explanation is: when *the True One* is necessarily-attached and stable to anything, that thing is, by necessity, *existent* and *eternal* — since it has been established that the non-existent is not described as one or many; so once the meaning of *the True One* has been deserved and stably attached to a thing, that thing has deserved the name and meaning of *existence*. Likewise, the meaning of *eternity* necessarily-attaches to it: for the True One cannot come-to-be, perish, transmute, or change — therefore He is eternal, since there is no first for Him. So one to whom the meaning of pure unity has been soundly established, the meaning of existence and eternity is, by that, necessarily-attached.

In the same way I say: when *the attribute of absolute existence* is necessarily-attached to a thing, the attribute of *the True One* and the attribute of *eternity* are necessarily-attached to it along with it. For absolute existence cannot be existence-after-non-existence; nor does it transmute from a state of existence into non-existence, nor from non-existence into existence; and what is so cannot be many — for *the many* is not found at absolute existence (I mean a continuous, permanent existence), on account of the priority of the *one* to it. So every absolutely-existent is not many — and is, therefore, one. And likewise it also deserves the attribute of eternity, for the absolutely-existent has no first and no last — so the meaning of eternity necessarily-attaches to it. And likewise I say that the attribute of *eternity* necessarily-attaches the attribute of *the True One* and *the attribute of absolute existence* to whatever deserves it. As for its deserving the attribute of *the True One*: absolute existence is that which has no beginning, and what has no beginning is not multiple — for every multiple has a first, and that is *the one*. So the multiple is not eternal; the eternal cannot be other than one. So the attribute of *one* is necessarily-attached upon the establishment of the attribute of *eternity*. And likewise the attribute of *existence* is necessarily-attached upon the establishment of the attribute of eternity, for the non-existent is not described as eternal or as originated.

So it has been made clear that these three attributes are *one* in their meaning and *one* in their referent; that they do not entail otherness in the essence of the Creator (exalted be He), nor the entry of accidents upon Him, nor multiplication of His meaning — since the purpose we grasp from them is that the Creator (exalted be He) is *not non-existent*, *not originated*, *not multiple*.

If it had been possible for us to express His meaning by a *single word* gathering these attributes at one stroke, so that these three meanings would be brought together in our intellects by a single word in the manner in which the three attributes we have mentioned bring them together for the intellect, we would have expressed Him by it. But since we have not found, in the languages by which we express ourselves, a single word that points to the true reality of the meaning of the Creator, we have drawn out the single meaning into more than a single word. So the multiplication that is found in the attributes of the Creator (exalted be He) is not on account of His essence, but only on account of the *deficiency* in the expressive capacity of the one who describes — to express His meaning by a word that points to it.

Understand, regarding the meaning of the Creator (exalted be He), that nothing is like Him; and whatever attributes you describe Him with, understand from them *the denial of their contrary from Him*. For this reason Aristotle said: *the negatives among the attributes of the Creator (exalted be He) are truer than the affirmatives*. For everything that is affirmed of Him from the attributes is not free from being [drawn from] attributes of substance or of accident — and the Creator of substance and accident does not have any attribute of *theirs* attaching to Him in His essence. But whatever is denied of Him in the attributes is, inevitably, true, and is fitting for Him — since He is loftier than every attribute and characterization, higher than every likeness and resemblance.
Therefore you ought to understand from these three intelligible attributes that we have mentioned *only* the denial of their contraries from the Creator (exalted be He).

As for the *active* divine attributes: they are the descriptions by which the Creator (exalted be He) is described on account of His effects — descriptions in which He may share with some of His creatures. It was permitted to describe Him by them out of the necessity of making Him known and of [our] standing upon His existence, so that we might be in a position to bind ourselves to His obedience. The use of this category of attributes of the Creator (exalted be He) is frequent in God's Book and in the books of His prophets, and in the praises of prophets and friends [of God] to God (exalted be He).

It is also of two kinds. One of them: descriptions that signify shape and bodily form — such as the Book's "And God created man in His image" (Genesis 1:27), "in the image of God He made man" (Genesis 9:6), "by the mouth of the Lord" (Numbers 9:18), "I, My hands stretched out the heavens" (Isaiah 45:12), "in the ears of the Lord" (Numbers 11:1), "and under His feet" (Exodus 24:10), "Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord" (Isaiah 51:9), "in which He has not lifted up My soul to vanity" (Psalm 24:4), "in the eyes of the Lord" (e.g., Genesis 6:8), "and the Lord said in His heart" (Genesis 8:21) — and the like of these, from the bodily limbs.

The second kind: bodily *motions and actions* — such as "And God saw the light" (Genesis 1:4), "And the Lord regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He grieved in His heart" (Genesis 6:6), "And the Lord smelled" (Genesis 8:21), "And God remembered" (Genesis 8:1), "And the Lord heard" (Numbers 11:1), "and the Lord awoke as one out of sleep" (Psalm 78:65) — and many like these, from the actions of rational beings.

Yet our early ones (peace be upon them), in their interpretation of the Holy Books, translated this category of the Creator's attributes for us with the most delicate sense possible, ascribing them to *the Glory of the Lord* (*kavod Adonai*) — as they translated "And behold, the Lord stood beside him" (Genesis 28:13) as "Behold, the Glory of the Lord stood"; "And God went up from him" (Genesis 35:13) — "And the Glory of the Lord was lifted up from him"; "And the Lord came down" (Exodus 19:20) — "And the Glory of the Lord revealed itself." They brought them out by a fine course, and denied them from the Creator (mighty and exalted), so that nothing of corporealization and accidence would attach to the Maker.

The eminent leader, our master Saadia Gaon (may God be pleased with him) has been at length in setting out this meaning in the *Book of Beliefs and Convictions*, in the commentary on the *Order of Bereshit*, in the commentary on the *Order of Va-Era*, and in the *Book of Creation* — to a degree that obviates the need to expound them in this book of mine.

What we summarize is: necessity drove [the Scriptures] to *the corporealization* of the Creator and to describing Him by attributes of the creatures, in order to establish in souls the meaning of *the existence of the Creator*. So the prophetic books expressed this for people in bodily expressions that draw near to their intellects and their understandings. Were the books to have described Him by *spiritual* expressions and *spiritual* concepts proper to Him — we would have remained ignorant of both the word and the meaning, and obedience to one whose meaning is unknown is not valid. Hence it was necessary that the word and the meaning conform to the listener's understanding, that the meaning may fall in his *wahm* — first in accordance with the corporeal sense understood from the corporealized word; then he is to be refined with it, and acquainted with the fact that *what was expressed in the Book was an approximation and a manner of speech*, and the true meaning is finer, higher, nobler, and remoter than what could be grasped according to the delicacy of His meaning.

So the discerning rational man strives to *strip the husks of the word and its corporeality* from the meaning, and to ascend by his *wahm* from rank to rank within it, until what is in his capacity and his apprehension of the true reality of the meaning sought is brought to fulfillment. The dull-witted ignorant person firmly believes in the Creator according to the outward expression of the Book — but if he binds himself to his Lord's obedience and exerts himself to act in accord with His desire, his excuse on the side of his ignorance and the small extent of his understanding is broad. For the human being is not held to account except in accord with his capacity and his apprehension in his intellect, his discernment, his strength, and his means. Yet the ignorant one, if it is possible for him to learn the science and he is heedless of it, is held to account and punished for his shortfall and for his sitting back from seeking it.

Were the Book to have proceeded in its expression of this matter in the course that suits its true reality of meaning — which only the discerning rational person grasps — most of the rational beings would have remained without religion and without law, on account of the dullness of their understanding and the weakness of their discernment from spiritual matters. So the address that is understood with a *bodily* meaning does not harm the rational person, on account of his discernment beyond it, and benefits the ignorant person, by establishing in his soul that he has a Creator whom he is obligated to obey.

This is like one to whom a man of means comes as a guest, obliged to host him — and who has draught animals he must feed: he sends [his host] much barley to feed his animals, and a small amount of food fit for the man himself, only as much as suffices for his nourishment. Likewise, language has expanded — and so have all the books of the prophets and the reports of the friends [of God] — concerning the descriptions of the Creator (mighty and exalted) by these corporeal expressions we have mentioned, in accord with the understandings of the multitude and the way the common people address one another. That is why our early ones said on this matter: "*The Torah speaks in the language of the children of men*" (b. Berakhot 31b).

And the Books have given hints, *by way of indication only*, at the spiritual meanings that those who possess intellects and understanding can grasp — that the totality may be on a level in *knowing the existence of the Creator* (exalted be He), even if the true reality of His essence varies in their intellects. The same applies to every refined meaning in the Book of God — like the recompense of the next world and its retribution. The same applies to the explanation of the inward science that I have intended to set forth in this book of mine.

For the Book restricted itself in its expression of [these matters], relying on those who have intellects, and gave indication of them by way of allusion — and we have mentioned these in the preface to this book of mine — so that the one for whom investigation of it and its seeking is possible would be alerted to it, and reach it, and grasp it, as the friend [of God] said: "And those who seek the Lord understand all things" (Proverbs 28:5).

And the Messenger (peace be upon him) safeguarded us, and warned us not to depict any form or likeness or resemblance for our Creator (mighty and exalted), in his saying: "Take therefore good heed unto your souls, for you saw no form…" (Deuteronomy 4:15), and: "And you saw no form; there was only a voice" (Deuteronomy 4:12). He intends by his saying "Take very good heed unto your souls" — preserve yourselves, by your *wahms* and your thoughts, from likening any model to the Creator (mighty and exalted), and from depicting for Him any form or resemblance; since your visions did not light upon any shape or any form at the time of His address to you. And He said: "To whom, then, will you liken God, or what likeness will you compare unto Him?" (Isaiah 40:18); and: "'To whom, then, will you liken Me, that I should be equal?' says the Holy One" (Isaiah 40:25); and the friend [of God] said: "For who in the sky can be compared unto the Lord? Who among the sons of the mighty can be likened to the Lord?" (Psalm 89:7); and: "There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours" (Psalm 86:8); and many of the like.

And on account of the impossibility of depicting Him in the intellects, and of representing Him in the imaginings — we find that the Book ascribes most of its praises and its glorifications to *the Name of the Creator* (mighty and exalted), such as: "And let them bless the name of Your glory" (Nehemiah 9:5); "to fear the honored and awful Name" (Deuteronomy 28:58); "And because of My name He is fearful" (Malachi 2:5); "But to you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness shall arise" (Malachi 3:20); "Sing unto the Lord, sing praises to His name; extol Him who rides upon the heavens by His name *Yah*" (Psalm 68:5). All of this is in glorification, magnification, and exaltation of the essence of the Creator (exalted be He) — since in our *wahms*, after [our acknowledging] His existence, there is nothing valid except His sublime and lofty Name alone. As for His essence and the true reality of His meanings, no form, no shape, no likeness for them exists in our thoughts and imaginings. That is why His Name is repeated so frequently in His Book and in the books of His prophets — for we conceive nothing of Him beyond His existence and His Name.

The Books have ascribed Him to the heavens and the earth, and to the world and to the spirits — like the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him): "And I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of the heavens and the God of the earth" (Genesis 24:3); and the saying of Jonah: "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of the heavens, who has made the sea and the dry land" (Jonah 1:9); and the saying of the Messenger (peace be upon him): "Let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, set a man over the congregation" (Numbers 27:16); and His own saying (exalted): "Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh" (Jeremiah 32:27). The cause of this is that He is made known to us mostly *from the side of what we have grasped of Him by our intellect and our understanding of His meaning*.

We also find Him made known to us frequently by way of *our fathers* (peace be upon them) — as: "The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has appeared to me…" (Exodus 3:16); and: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you" (Exodus 3:15). The reason is that He is made known to us from the side of what we have stood upon of Him — namely, the transmission of the fathers, the proper way of life that we have inherited from them, as the Book said: "For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice" (Genesis 18:19). It may also be that He was made known by them because of their distinction in worship of God in their time — for the people of their age were worshippers of other than God. The same applies to His being called "the God of the Hebrews" (Exodus 3:18) and "the God of Israel" (e.g., Exodus 5:1) — as is said: "Not as these is the portion of Jacob, for He is the Former of all" (Jeremiah 10:16); and the friend [of God] said: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup" (Psalm 16:5).

If we had been able to apprehend the true reality of His meaning, He would not have made Himself known to us by anything else. Since the apprehension of the true reality of His meaning was impossible for our intellects, He has described Himself as *the Lord of the most noble of His creatures*, rational and non-rational. That is why He said to the Messenger (peace be upon him) — when [Moses] asked of Him "And they will say, 'What is His name?' What shall I say to them?" — He answered him: "*Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: *Ehyeh* has sent me to you" (Exodus 3:13–14). When [God] knew that the people would not grasp the true reality of this name from this expression, He added a clarification, saying after it: "And God further said to Moses: Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: *The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, has sent me to you*.
