This is My name forever, and this is My memorial for all generations" (Exodus 3:15) — meaning by this: *Since the people are ignorant of this name and its meaning by way of their intellects, I declare to them that I am the One they know from the side of the transmission of their fathers.* For the Creator (exalted be He) has set down no path to His knowledge but these two: one is *the intelligible*, by way of His manifest traces in His creatures; the second is *the transmitted*, by way of the fathers and the righteous predecessors — as the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "What wise men have told, and have not hid from their fathers" (Job 15:18).

And since our apprehension of every existent thing comes only from one of three sides — the first being our bodily senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch); the second being the way of our intellects, which is the gate of inference upon the existing thing from its traces and acts, so that we ascertain the soundness of its existence and the true reality of its meaning by the soundness of what we have apprehended by our senses (and this is what is called in the Book *knowledge and instruction of the intellect* (Proverbs 1:2)); the third being *the truthful report* and *the sound transmission* — and since the apprehension of the Creator (exalted be He) is impossible from the side of our senses, His apprehension is permitted only from the side of *the truthful report* and from the side of *the inference upon Him from His traces*.

So when the inference from the side of His traces in the creatures became established for us, and these proved to be too many for the multiplicity of the attributes of the Creator (mighty and exalted) that arise from them to be encompassed — the prophets and the friends [of God] described Him by various descriptions. Among them is the description of the Messenger (peace be upon him): "The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are judgment" (Deuteronomy 32:4); and again: "For the Lord your God, He is God of gods, and Lord of lords; the great, mighty, and awful God, who does not show favor and does not take bribes; who executes the judgment of the orphan and the widow, and loves the stranger" (Deuteronomy 10:17–18); and He (exalted) said, in describing His way among the creatures: "The Lord, the Lord, merciful and gracious God, slow to anger and abundant in mercy and truth, keeping mercy unto thousands" (Exodus 34:6–7). All of these are attributes inferred from His traces in His creatures, and from the wisdom and power manifest in His works.

When we seek something of this meaning by our intellects and our discernment, we fall short of grasping the smallest part of the parts of His descriptions and praises — as the friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "Many are the wonderful works which You have done, O Lord my God, and Your thoughts toward us…" (Psalm 40:6), and: "Who can express the mighty acts of the Lord? Who can make all His praise to be heard?" (Psalm 106:2), and: "And let them bless the name of Your glory, that is exalted above all blessing and praise" (Nehemiah 9:5). And in the transmission of our fathers (peace be upon them): "*A certain prayer-leader who went down before R. Ḥanina said: 'The God, the great, the mighty, the awful, the powerful, the strong, the bold.' He said to him: 'Have you concluded all the praises of your Master? Even these three — "great, mighty, and awful" — had Moses not said them, and the men of the Great Assembly come and instituted them in the prayer, we would not say them. And yet you praise Him this much? Parable: of a king of flesh and blood who had thousands upon thousands of golden dinars, and they praised him with silver — is that not a disgrace to him?*'" (b. Berakhot 33b). And he said: "*To You, silence is praise, O God, in Zion*" (Psalm 65:2). And [the rabbis] said: "*The medicine of all is silence*" — "Parable: of a precious pearl beyond price; the more you praise it, the more you cheapen it."

So you ought, my brother, to exert yourself, and bind yourself to *making the acquaintance* of the true reality of your Creator (mighty and exalted) *from the side of His traces, not from the side of His essence*. For He is the nearest of all near things on the side of His traces, and the most remote of all remote things on the side of the representation of His essence and His depiction — since He has no existence in our *wahms* by any of these aspects, as we have set out. So when you reach the point of bringing Him out of your *wahm* and your sense-perception, as if He had no existence, and finding Him from the side of His traces as if He never separates from you — that is the utmost in knowing Him, the knowing that the Messenger urged when he said: "And you shall know this day, and bring back to your heart, that the Lord, He is God" (Deuteronomy 4:39).

One of the knowers said: *The most knowing of people of God is the most bewildered in Him*. And it was said: *The most knowing of people of God is the most ignorant of the true reality of His essence; the most ignorant of Him is the most knowing in his own opinion of the true reality of His essence.*

A certain one of them was asked about God. He said: "God is one." The questioner said: "How is He?" He answered: "A great king." The questioner said: "Where is He?" He answered: "Always at the ready." The questioner said: "It is not about this that I asked you." He said: "Your question — in these expressions — concerns only the attributes that fit the creature, not the Creator. As for the attributes that we must verify of our Creator (exalted be He): I have already told you what I told you, [and] there is no way for us to anything other than that."

It is told of one of the righteous that he used to say in his intimate prayer: *O Lord, where do I find You? Indeed, where do I not find You?* You have hidden Yourself, and You are not seen; yet the All is full of You — corresponding to His saying: "Do I not fill heaven and earth? — declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 23:24).

So the utmost in knowing Him is your acknowledgment and your certainty that you are in the utmost ignorance of the true reality of His essence. So when a form is represented in your *wahm*, or a likeness in your thought, employ the way of *investigation* into His meaning, and His existence will continue to be ascertained for you, while every likeness for Him is excluded from your *wahm* — until you find Him only by way of inference. The nearest of the examples for this, by way of approximation and expression: our finding the true reality of *the soul*, without our apprehending for it form, shape, color, or scent — despite the fame of its actions and the manifest appearance of its traces in us. Likewise, *the intellect*: despite the manifest appearance of its traces and the clarity of its actions, we do not apprehend for it form or likeness in our thoughts. *A fortiori* the Creator of the All, who has nothing like Him.
The Philosopher said: *If discursive reasoning is cut off short of the soul, how much more must it be cut off short of the Maker* (mighty and exalted).

And since we have reached this point in our discourse, we have no need to set forth this matter further — out of caution and dread before it. And one of the learned has said: "Do not seek what is too wondrous for you, do not investigate what is hidden from you; in what is permitted to you, contemplate — you have no business in the hidden things" (cf. b. Ḥagigah 13a, citing Ben Sira 3:21–22). And they have said: *Anyone who has not had concern for the honor of his Maker — better that he had not come into the world*. And he said: "Shall it be told to Him when I speak — or shall a man wish to be devoured?" (Job 37:20); and they said: "*If a man comes to recount the mighty acts of the Holy One, blessed be He, he is swallowed up from the world*" (cf. b. Megillah 18a). And the Book said: "And He smote the men of Beit Shemesh, because they had looked into the ark of the Lord" (1 Samuel 6:19). The friend [of God] (peace be upon him) said: "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing" (Proverbs 25:2) — that is, the concealing of His secret from the multitude. And David (peace be upon him) said: "The secret of the Lord is to those who fear Him" (Psalm 25:14).

What you ought to verify is: the bodily senses we have mentioned, and the *soul-senses* — namely, memory, thought, conjecture, opinion, and discernment — all end at a single meaning: namely, *the intellect*, which supplies them with the power to apprehend meanings. Each one of these senses has a special object it apprehends and does not apprehend anything else — like the colors and shapes which we apprehend only by the sense of sight; and sounds and tunes, which we apprehend only by the sense of hearing; the scents and the kinds of smelled-things, by the sense of smell; the kinds of tastes, by the sense of taste; heat and cold and many qualities, by the sense of touch only. Each of these senses has a power for apprehending its sense-object up to a *bounded distance*, at the end of which it stops. As with sight: it apprehends the seen at a proximity to it; the further away the seen is from the seer, the weaker the apprehension, until sight stops and does not apprehend the seen. The same with hearing, and with the rest of the senses. There is no way to apprehend a sense-object by anything other than the sense prepared for it. Whoever attempts this, the object sought goes lacking when he seeks it — as one who attempts to apprehend tunes by his sight, colors by his hearing, tastes by his touch: the things go lacking in their existence for him, even though they are existent for one who seeks them by the instruments by which they are to be apprehended.

The same holds for the *soul-senses* we have mentioned: each one of them has a certain power for apprehending a certain sense-object, not to be apprehended by anything else, and has a certain limit at which the sense, having reached, stops. Likewise the *intellect*: it apprehends intelligible things by its own essence and by the way of inference. What is near, it apprehends by the true reality of its essence; what is far and hidden from its apprehension, it apprehends by the way of inference. Since the Creator (mighty and exalted) is the most hidden of all hidden things and the most remote of all remote things — from the side of His essence — for us, the intellect apprehends nothing of Him except the meaning of His existence alone. Whoever attempts to apprehend the true reality of His essence or to liken Him, [in his apprehension] the existent he had ascertained goes lacking — for he has attempted what is not in his strength, in line with what we have described concerning the bodily sense-object that goes lacking when sought without the appropriate sense.

So we ought to seek the existence of the Creator (exalted be He) from the side of His traces in the creatures, and infer from them upon Him. And once His existence has been established for us from this side, we ought to stop and not seek, in our thoughts, His depiction, nor in our imaginings His representation and individuation and apprehension of the depth of His essence. For when we do this — supposing that this brings Him near to our understandings — we make His existence go lacking; for every represented thing in our *wahms* is the meaning of *something other than Him*. As the Wise One said: "Have you found honey? Eat what is sufficient for you, lest you be sated and vomit it out" (Proverbs 25:16).

I shall bring this meaning near to you by two close examples. The first will show you that every sense has the power to apprehend its own sense-object up to a limit, and then it stops; another sense then takes over after it and, in turn, stops; and so with the rest. When the senses stop, the intellect takes over apprehension of what lies within its power — and all of this concerning *one and the same* meaning.

Suppose a thrown stone, at a distance, has a sound; it has struck a certain person. By the sense of sight, he has apprehended the color and shape of the stone; by the sense of hearing, the sound of the stone; by the sense of touch, its coldness and roughness. Then the bodily senses stop, and they grasp nothing more from the stone's case. *Then the intellect apprehends* that the stone has a thrower who threw it — since it has been established that the stone did not move from itself. So whatever was *in the way of being apprehended by the bodily senses* is impossible for the intellect to apprehend without them — and *a fortiori* the bodily senses cannot reach what is in the way of being apprehended *by the intellect alone*. So if the apprehension of the depth of the essence of the Creator (exalted be He) is impossible for our intellects, how should it be permitted to us to represent Him and to delimit Him and to depict Him and to liken Him with anything from the apprehensions of our bodily senses? That is impossible.

The second example shows that, with spiritual matters whose existence we have ascertained, prudence does not lie in *pursuing* them and investigating their *essence* — for this corrupts our intellects. That is like one who would attempt to apprehend the sun from the side of its light, its rays, its shining, and the denial of darkness from it: he stands upon the soundness of its existence, benefits from it, makes use of the light of its illumination, and reaches the desired end from it. But one who attempts to apprehend the sun from the side of its disk and to fix his sight upon the eye of the sun — his sight is veiled, his light is lost, and he derives no benefit from the sun.

The same is the case for us when we apprehend the existence of the Creator (exalted be He) from the side of His traces, and His wisdom in them, and His power in His creatures: we have understood Him, we have grasped His meaning. At that point our intellects are illumined by the knowing of Him and the apprehension of all that is in our intellects to apprehend — as He has said: "I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your benefit, who leads you in the way you should go" (Isaiah 48:17). But when we attempt by our intellects to apprehend the meaning of *His essence* and its depiction and its representation in our *wahms*, we lose our intellects and our discernment, and we apprehend nothing of what we know by them — as happens to our sights when we look attentively at the eye of the sun. So we ought to be wary of this matter, and to keep it in mind when investigating the meaning of the existence of the Creator (exalted be He).

Likewise we ought to safeguard ourselves concerning His descriptions — with which He has described Himself, and with which His friends [of God] have described Him — that we not firmly believe them according to the outward sense of the word and the literal meaning of the bodily expression. Rather, it is incumbent upon us to know, with sound and certain knowledge, that they are *metaphors and expressions* in accord with our discernment and what our understandings and intellects can bear — on account of the necessity of being acquainted with Him and of magnifying His glory; and He (exalted) is loftier and more sublime than all of that, to a degree without limit, in line with what the Book said: "And exalted above all blessing and praise" (Nehemiah 9:5).

One of the philosophers said: *Those whose understanding has fallen short of explicating the meanings of the simples have clung to the names by which the revealed Books have spoken concerning the Maker — not realizing that the addresses in the books of the religious laws are by the measure of the understandings of those upon whom they were sent down, not by the measure of what can be encompassed by the One who addresses them.* They are like the whistle to a draught animal at watering — by which it is urged to drink more than it would be urged by addressing the animal in finer speech.

So when you have, my brother, stood at this rank of *tawḥīd* by your intellect and your understanding — purify yourself for the Creator (mighty be His Name), strive in apprehending His existence from the side of His wisdom, His power, His tenderness, His mercy, and the intensity of His care for the creatures — and make these your means to Him. Then you will be among the seekers of the Lord (cf. Ps 24:6), and you will receive from Him aid and reinforcement toward understanding Him and apprehending the true reality of His meaning, as the prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The secret of the Lord is for those who fear Him, and His covenant — to make them know" (Psalm 25:14). I shall expound for you exemplars in Gate Two of this book of mine; if you take them up and walk by their road, this will be made easy upon you, if God wills.
As for the *corrupters* of the purification of affirming-the-unity for God — they are many. Among them is *associationism* with God, which is of various kinds.

Among them is the doctrine of the people of *two* and the people of *three*. Among them is the worship of images and of the sun and the moon and the stars and the fire and plants and animals. Among them is firmly believing in the corporealization of the Creator (exalted be He) after [one has reached] knowledge of the purpose of the Book's use of [such language] for Him. Among them is *hidden associationism* — that is, ostentation in religious acts before people; and this is of many varieties, which I shall set forth in Gate Five of this book, with the help of God (exalted be He). Among them is the inclination, with desire, toward the disgraceful appetites of the bodies — for this is hidden associationism, since the human being is associating, with the worship of his Lord, the worship of his own desire — as the Book said: "Let there be no strange god in you" (Psalm 81:10), and our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "*Who is the strange god that is in a man's body? — say: this is the evil inclination*" (b. Shabbat 105b).

Perhaps a dull-witted ignorant one, when he reads this book of mine and stops upon what we have mentioned in this gate, will say: *Is the meaning of God's unity hidden from anyone who has read a single page of God's Book — that this [author] should alert us to it and guide us toward it?* I say in answer to him what the Wise One has counseled: "Answer a fool in line with his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes" (Proverbs 26:5). For the speaker of this statement is weak in discernment from grasping that a general thing, when it falls upon different kinds, is received by them differently — by more and less, stronger and weaker.

The example: the generality of the light of the sun for the people of the earth. We find that they divide concerning it into three divisions. The first: people of clear vision, whose sights are sound and free of every defect; they benefit by the sun, make use of its illumination, and accomplish their needs by it. The second division: the blind, whose sight has wholly departed; the sun neither benefits nor harms them, but they receive its benefit only by intermediaries. The third division: people whose sight has grown weak in [its capacity to] make use of the sun, so that it harms their sight if they do not veil it from the sun's illumination. But if they hasten to treat their sight with eye-medicines, salves, and the refinement of their nourishment, while taking care to guard their sight from working in sun-light — they will join the sound and benefit from the sun, which had been harming them. And if they are heedless of the treatment, they will quickly join the rank of the blind, and the light of their sight will depart.

On this example, the meaning of *tawḥīd* — set forth in God's truthful Book — is divided among the ranks of the rational beings, even though it is universal to them all (as the sun's light is universal to all who possess sight, as we have described). Their understanding of it varies in three divisions. The first: people of pure intellects and brilliant native abilities; the second: people whose intellects have grown weak from discerning the contents of God's Book *altogether*; the third: people whose intellects have grown weak below the intellects of the first rank, but who have strength to discern most of the closer, easier matters.

The first rank — namely, people of sound intellects from defects — when they understand what has come down upon them in God's Book concerning *tawḥīd*, are guided to it, and its meaning is brought to completion in their souls by the strength of their minds and the purity of their intellects. Such people have no need of this book of mine, except as a reminder of what they have been heedless of. As for the second rank: they have no knowledge of God's Book, let alone of the *tawḥīd* set out in it; they hear only its report and grasp nothing of its meaning. There is for them no benefit and no harm in my book. As for the third rank: they understand the *tawḥīd* of God's Book somewhat, but their discernment is not strong enough to grasp its meaning and to stand upon its true reality. If a guide leads them toward it and they grasp its meaning by way of the true demonstrations and the rational evidences, they verify its meaning, its profit is made plain to them, and they join the first rank. But if they are heedless of investigation and speculative inquiry into what would strengthen their discernment and polish their intellects — they fall to the rank of the ignorant. This book of mine is profitable for this rank, with a profit general and comprehensive, on account of the possibility of investigation for them. It is for them in the place of useful eye-medicines for those of weak sight, who are healed by their treatment.

The Book has likened the ignorant to the blind, and wisdom to light, and likened ignorance to darkness, in His saying: "And I also saw that wisdom excels folly, as light excels darkness" (Ecclesiastes 2:13); and: "The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness" (Ecclesiastes 2:14); and: "The deaf, hear; and the blind, look on, to see" (Isaiah 42:18). And the Book has likened knowledge and culture to the tree of life, as he said: "She is a tree of life to those who hold her" (Proverbs 3:18), and: "For they are life to those who find them" (Proverbs 4:22).
May God guide us to the path of His knowledge, and direct us to His obedience, and grant us success in what pleases Him, by His mercy. Amen.
